📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over a year into her tenure as CBS News’ Editor-in-Chief, Bari Weiss has sought to move the storied organization into a latest era. Those attempts have apparently come with some growing pains, however, as the network has seen staffing changes and fluctuating ratings in recent months. At the same time, drama has been swirling around Weiss due to her reported vision for the brand and editorial decisions she’s made. Now, the firm is experiencing more major staffing shakeups months after those 60 Minutes exits.

Sources indicate that in the aftermath of the Paramount Skydance/Warner Bros. Discovery merger, the media conglomerate Skydance has been born, and further consolidation is on the horizon. The new company recently offered buyouts to employees at CBS News, and dozens of employees reportedly accepted the deals. Status (via The Daily Beast) reports that different departments within the Eye Network’s news branch were impacted, including CBS Evening News, CBS Mornings, 60 Minutes and the company’s news bureaus.

A source spoke out about this major development, saying “It’s pretty much an extinction-level event.” That particular insider was apparently from the London bureau, which has reportedly been hit the hardest by the buyouts. As for the cause of this, it’s said that London-based employees had been displeased with Foreign Editor Shayndi Raice since she allegedly called out staffers for “insubordination.” Concerns about CBS News being merged with (the recently acquired) CNN are also said to have factored into these staff exits.

How Bari Weiss Responded After Being Asked If She’d Like To Run CNN.

What’s also notable about this situation is that it comes on the heels of a significant development regarding CBS News’ Face the Nation. Senior executive producer Mary Hager is leaving the show and the network after having worked there for 35 years. (It’s unclear whether Hager’s departure has to do with her accepting a buyout.) Additionally, executive producer Anne Hsu is leaving as well for a new gig with the network’s Hong Kong bureau. So Weiss now finds herself in the position to reshape the show after allegedly having considered firing host Margaret Brennan earlier this year.

It’s also worth mentioning how this round of buyouts has apparently impacted 60 Minutes. Per the report, more than a half dozen employees opted to take buyouts, yet none of those were reportedly senior-level employees. Yet this marks yet another change at the manufacturer amid continued headlines about declining ratings in the aftermath of this summer’s staffing changes.

Weiss and 60 Minutes executive producer Nick Bilton made some major changes to the news magazine show on May 28, 2026 (which is allegedly known as “Black Thursday” within the manufacturer). On that day, the company officially parted ways with veteran correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega as well as EP Tanya Simon and others for reasons that have still yet to be specified. And, shortly after that, another seasoned correspondent – Scott Pelley – was fired after a heated meeting with Bilton. It was during that conversation that Pelley allegedly accused Weiss of “murdering” the show.

Those high-profile firings aren’t the only controversies that have swirled around 60 in recent months. As has been the case with other CBS News programs as of late, the show has seen viewership numbers that have come in below the averages of the previous season. On top of that, some former staffers continue to criticize Weiss’ leadership, and they’ve made claims about editorial bias under her direction. Weiss and co. have denied claims of editorial interference, and some staffers have praised her approach to her job.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Still, Bari Weiss did recently address concerns regarding 60 Minutes, and she declared that the show had been doing “tremendously well.” There reportedly remain concerns, however, about what lies ahead for the show and CBS News as a whole. At this point, questions remain, especially amid these recent staffing shakeups due to the buyouts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fuse Games, the developer of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, has mentioned it "didn't dream" the pod racing game's background character Biddy Blas would become as popular as he has.

Since Galactic Racer's release in October, Blas - who resembles a short, humanoid crocodile (officially a crocin) - has become a viral sensation. The combination of his unexpected swagger and ridiculous high-pitched Huttese monologues - performed irresistibly by actor Richard Summers-Calvert - have made him a fan favourite, especially his catchphrase "scrib doon" (which means "write it down").

According to recent reports, "Here's a name for you, amateur!" Blas tells the player upon meeting them, albeit in Huttese. "Biddy Blas. Write it down. Tattoo it on your arm, and someday your arm will be worth millions!".

Recent findings suggest that fuse Games shared a comment from Biddy Blas creator and Galactic Racer narrative designer Ren Alex-Rose about the character's success. "We always suspected Biddy Blas would be a popular member of the Galactic League, but we didn't dream of just how popular he'd become," Alex-Rose remarked.

"He was an incredibly enjoyable character to build, from our early ideation of a small, angry non-human character (who we lovingly referred to as our cast's 'chaos goblin') to recording his sometimes-absurdist dialogue with Blas' voice actor, who took the crocin to a whole new level.

It has been revealed that "It's been great watching Biddy Blas emerge into his assured self, as well as seeing the community embrace him for it. He's always known exactly who he is, and he wears it proudly.".

Blas' breakout success was praised by Lucasfilm producer Craig Derrick, who noted his social feeds were filled with posts about Galactic Racer, though mostly about Biddy Blas. And the enthusiasm actor Richard Summers-Calvert was greeted with during October's MCM Comic-Con in London, which I attended, was palpable. There's a nice video of him doing Blas' voice on Instagram.

According to recent reports, star Wars: Galactic Racer was awarded a full five stars in Eurogamer's review. "Both a surprisingly fun Roguelite campaign and a racing treat for Criterion fans, this is just wonderful stuff," wrote Christian Donlan.

One thing I'm always curious about with games like this, however, is how much of that detail is on the surface versus what's actually happening under the hood.

I'm still too early in the game to judge this for myself, but according to Rockstar, there is way more going on in terms of how NPCs behave than players will ever likely see. One striking example of this is how GTA 6's gang compounds conduct their drug operations. In an interview with IGN, Rockstar's senior design director for its open world Steven Messinger explained that GTA 6 fully simulates drug distribution from top to bottom.

Recent findings suggest that "A big part of [the open world's design] was establishing deep backstories for almost everything, even if they were never meant to be fully explained to the player, and then really sticking to those backstories," Messinger pointed out. "For example, our gang compounds have a complex drug network we've fully mapped out: where the drugs come from, who brings them in and how, how they're distributed to each compound, what happens at each stop, and how they eventually reach the street-level buyer.".

According to recent reports, messinger notes that "players will only pick up bits and pieces of this". But representing this process wholesale means that, when players do notice it, it always feels authentic and believable. "Having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this massive machine is always running even when players aren't there.".

While this may only be designed for players to notice passively, I'm now keen to follow this system and see just how consistently it holds up. But it's such commitment to representing its world that has led GTA 6 to receive near-universal praise from critics, and it probably didn't hurt when it earned $3.79 billion on launch day, either.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of the best things to emerge from Grand Theft Auto over the years has been the community's truly spectacular stunts: players soaring under bridges, leaping across buildings, and more. And with GTA 6's release this week, we've seen the first signs of the trend continuing in a brand-new world.

Sources indicate that this TikTok video by user Gstitz from early in GTA 6, for instance, claims to be the "world's first" demonstration of a Mallard flying sideways between a narrow gap in a large building. It takes several attempts, but they eventually pull off the stunt without crashing or broken parts.

According to recent reports, another video from Hazardous is a more grounded (literally) look at Grand Theft Auto 6, and reveals the YouTuber flinging motorbikes and cars around the map as they explore promising high-risk jumps. Some of these locations are tied to in-game challenges, so there are certainly breadcrumbs placed by Rockstar to encourage such ventures.

Recent findings suggest that granted, these are far from the truly absurd stunts we've seen in prior Grand Theft Auto games. But as a firing gun for the wider community, it's a great start. They're also among the most impressive things we've seen in GTA 6's opening week.

It's doubtless been an eventful few days though. Players have been entranced by the slapstick violence and in-game social media. Even UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the game, despite not having time to actually play it. Eurogamer editor-in-chief Chris Tapsell also came away impressed, lauding it in his five star GTA 6 review.

If you're playing the game and need some help, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough, and our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheat list.

Latest Update: Robert Pattinson Is the Fresh James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

Sources indicate that that is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

It has been revealed that A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

Daniel Craig, Casino Royale, 2006.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

It has been revealed that when Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Roger Moore, The Spy Who Loved Me, 1977.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

In a recent development, also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the manufacturer acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Industry observers note that pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

It has been revealed that also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this fresh installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the substantial screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave newly introduced world of brand deals, anything is possible.

I Found Out From The Director and Mckenna Grace My Favorite Sunrise On The Reaping Scene WAS Shot, But Cut

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minor spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Industry observers note that the Hunger Games movies (which are streaming with a Hulu subscription) have entertained audiences for over ten years, and we've got yet another book to screen adaptation in theaters now thanks to Francis Lawrence's Sunrise on the Reaping film. My favorite scene from the book was unfortunately cut from the prequel movie, and I had to ask both the director and actress Mckenna Grace about it.

I loved the Sunrise on the Reaping book, and was wildly impressed by how well it was adapted for film. Unfortunately, the scene where Maysilee kills a Gamemaker alongside District 4 career Maritte didn't make it. As you can see in the video above, I asked Francis Lawrence about this decision, where he confirmed the sequence was shot during principal photography. In his words:.

It's probably the most debated sequence that we had throughout the development process. What happens is, because of that action with the game makers and because of the fight that happens with Maysilee and Haymitch after, it was a fight that in the book is about implicit submission. And the argument that some of us had was that he was already no longer submitting. Like, you know, if you've been down to Sub A, if you've done the things that he's done without spoiler in this movie he's not submitting anymore. And so it didn't feel like it thematically fit.

Points were made. While it would have been awesome to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker, in the novel it's connected to her relationship with Haymitch. They have an argument afterward about him still implicitly submitting to The Capitol, and not killing the Gamemakers despite being the closest Tribute to them. As director Francis Lawrence told me, that confrontation between the District 12 tributes didn't make sense for the movie adaptation, especially after following Joseph Zada's protagonist as he attempted to break The Arena.

This sequence was indeed shot, so the debate about whether or not to include it in Sunrise on the Reaping extended to the post-production phase. As the director went on to tell me:.

We shot it. We even augmented the fight to be, tried to be about different things. And then that thematically didn't fit. And so we ended up cutting it from the movie, but I believe will be one of the deleted scenes that will be available.

It has been revealed that fingers crossed that we get to see this scene sometime in the future, via special features when the latest Hunger Games prequel is released to homes. This isn't the only change made to Sunrise on the Reaping, which included some references to Lucy Gray Baird from Songbirds and Snakes. Of course, I had to ask the actress who brought Maysilee to life about the cut sequence.

While interviewing the cast of the upcoming Hunger Games movie, I asked Mckenna Grace about Maysilee's cut scene. She spoke about the argument with Joseph Zada's Haymitch that followed the Gamemaker death, telling me:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sources indicate that that argument scene was one of my favorite things that I got to do because it was just Joe and I in the woods like screaming at each other. I think that what it was, was it didn't make sense for our characters to be split at that time because we didn't have enough time to repair it like they did in the book. And we didn't have the scene, you know, where they're splitting the sardines like in the book. And so it just didn't make, it didn't make sense for them to be so split at that time whenever their bond had just become so strong. Because they didn't get to reforge it and go and burn through the hedge together.

Points were made. As awesome as it would have been to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker with one of her poisoned darts, that sequence also complicated her relationship with Haymitch shortly before her death. Instead, Francis Lawrence and organization decided to keep the District 12 tributes as a united force until Mckenna Grace's character was killed by bird mutts. As such, the death and Haymitch's reaction are given extra emotional weight.

Adapting novels for film is a tough task, and there's always some content that ends up on the cutting room floor. Francis Lawrence has directed almost all of the Hunger Games movies, so he knows all too well what this process is like. While Sunrise on the Reaping's reviews were mixed, I think that it was a wildly successful film version of the devastating novel.

In a recent development, the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in theaters now as part of the 2026 movie release list. Panem is once again on the big screen, here's to hoping that we get another prequel from author Suzanne Collins soon.
